newsitem.title: USA: Insurers may face big claims from TWA disaster.
newsitem.headline: Insurers may face big claims from TWA disaster.

text.p: Insurers might be hit with massive product liability claims if U.S. investigators declared the crash of TWA flight 800 the result of a mechanical failure.
That's because an aircraft or component part manufacturer's liability is unlimited.
But an airline's liability on international flights is limited to just $75,000 per passenger under a treaty known as the Warsaw Convention, unless there is a finding of willful misconduct.

"No limit of liability applies to a manufacturer in suits by the passengers; where there is a limit of liability against an airline engaged in international transportation," said Desmond T. Barry Jr., an aviation insurance lawyer and partner with New York law firm Condon & Forsyth.
"If you have a manufacturer as a defendant, you've got unlimited liability. You don't have to prove willful misconduct, you only have to prove negligence," he said.
And that hurdle is much easier to overcome than the willful misconduct test for airlines, he said.
"The legal hurdle is much smaller if it's a product involved than if it were a bomb," he said. "If it were a bomb... it's a very difficult burden of proof."
"Plaintiffs lawyers are going to try to zero in on a manufacturing or design defect," he said.
Indeed, three lawsuits stemming from the July 17 crash that killed all 230 people on board were filed about a month ago by the firm of Kreindler & Kreindler.
The suits, which name Trans World Airlines Inc and Boeing Co as defendants, allege that a mechanical, structural and/or electrical failure caused the mid-air break-up of the airplane.
Each of the three lawsuits is reported to seek a total of $75 million in damages from Boeing and TWA.
If the families of the more than 200 passengers on board the flight each won judgments of $50 million, the liability would top $10 billion.
A London market source, however, called that estimate unrealistic and far too high.
However, by contrast, an airline's liability for 200 passengers under the Warsaw Convention would come to about $15 million.
And an airline's liability on domestic flights, which is generally estimated at about $2 million to $3 million per passenger, for 200 passengers could come to about $600 million.
TWA has liability coverage of $1 billion while Boeing has liability coverage of an aggregate $2 billion, according to London market sources. Boeing declined comment.
Lloyd's of London was a major participant in TWA's liability coverage and the Kiln Syndicate 955 led Boeing's liability policy.
But if investigators are unable to pinpoint the mechanical failure that caused the accident, such product liability claims may prove unsuccessful.
In that case, the liability would belong to TWA's insurers and the claims would fall within the $75,000 per person limit set by the Warsaw Convention, an aviation insurance expert said.

Those Warsaw Convention limits were exceeded in the Pan Am bombing case, after a jury found the airline guilty of negligence and willful misconduct because of its failure to implement security procedures that could have thwarted the bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland.
If the TWA disaster were also caused by a bomb, the liability would be limited by the Warsaw Convention unless there were a finding of willful misconduct.
Meanwhile, the missile theory moved back into center stage when former White House official Pierre Salinger said on Friday that a U.S. Navy missile accidentally shot down the TWA airliner.
The U.S. government denied that suggestion. James Kallstrom, head of the FBI in New York, said on Friday the so-called friendly fire theory was "total, unadulterated nonsense."
Under such a scenario, however, the U.S. taxpayer would pick up the tab for the accident, not insurers.
